text: I remember when my son was about 7, we had three jars on the kitchen counter. Spend, save, share. And he labeled them himself, very nicely. And every week he would divide his allowance between them. And the save one, he would put coins in there. And it was very slow, very slow, very slow. At first, he didn't like to save. He wanted a scooter. He was very far away from being able to buy it. And we made a chart and every Sunday, he would count his money and put a little sticker closer to the picture of the scooter that was on the end. And there were a few setbacks. Once he almost spent the entire jar for a pack of cards and we talked about wants now and wants later. And he put them back. The share jar was just to show that money also can go out. But the save jar was to show that you need to wait. And then after a few months, he bought the scooter. And it was so serious that I remember him going to the shop and paying the money. And it was very serious to him. And I think I learned more than him. I think that after that, I became more disciplined in spending money and I saw my impulse purchases a bit differently. Now the jars are gone, but the habit stays. That's why I say that habit is very strong, much stronger than any advice, any lecture, and so on. And I think that teaching a child to save, it's just a simple way to make the future look tangible.
